course_title: Proposal Writing: Grants and Business Proposals

say: From problem to plan: objectives, activities and project logic.
This is the video for module two of Proposal Writing.
The problem statement is the foundation of your proposal. Your objectives must fix the problem you describe, and your activities must tackle its causes.

say: And why does it happen? Name the root causes your project will tackle.
A common mistake is calling the lack of your solution the problem. No soap-making centre is not the problem. Low income is.

say: Your own data is often the most convincing evidence, because national figures rarely describe your ward. For example, Amaka surveyed 40 members of her cooperative in one week, with a one-page paper form. The course uses illustrative results.

say: Objectives are the specific changes your project will achieve and measure. Empower women economically sounds good, but it has no number and no date.

panel.heading: Weak objective or SMART objective?
left: Train many women in soap making

say: SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. Amaka writes: by month 3, 40 women complete 12 days of training.
By month 6, at least 30 sell their own products at least twice a month, and at least 25 report a monthly profit increase of 10,000 naira or more.
Be realistic, not impressive. Meeting a modest target builds a funder's trust.

say: Funders want to see why your activities should lead to the change you promise. Inputs are your resources. Activities are what you do with them.

panel.heading: The results chain
items: Inputs: money, people, materials
Activities: what you do
Outputs: what you deliver
Outcomes: the change in people
Impact: the long-term change

say: Outputs are what you deliver, fully under your control, like 40 women trained.

say: A theory of change is a chain of if, then statements. If 40 women get practical training, then they will have the skills to make good products. Assumption: they can attend 2 sessions a week.

panel.heading: Amaka's if-then chain
items: IF trained, THEN they can make good products
IF given starter kits, THEN no borrowing
IF mentored with market days, THEN they sell
IF they sell and track costs, THEN income rises

say: If they receive starter kits, then they can produce without borrowing. Assumption: materials stay close to budget prices.

say: If they sell and track costs, then their income will increase. Trainers turning up is not an assumption. That is your job.

panel.rule: An assumption is a condition outside your direct control.

say: A logframe puts the same logic into a table: goal, outcome, outputs and activities. Read across each row.
It needs a clear summary, one to three indicators with targets, a real source of evidence such as attendance sheets or surveys, and honest assumptions.
Use the funder's template if there is one.

panel.heading: Check every row of your logframe
items: A clear narrative summary
One to three indicators, each with a target
A real means of verification
Assumptions truly outside your control

say: Your practice. Draw a problem tree and collect at least one piece of evidence. Write a problem statement of 200 to 300 words. Write 2 or 3 SMART objectives with a simple workplan chart.
Then write your if-then chain and fill a logframe. Now continue with the lessons below.
